summary.text: 火 is a whole-character picture of light and flames rising from a burning object, used for ‘fire’. The image is not divided into smaller sound or meaning parts.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts light and flames rising from a burning object; it is not built from smaller semantic or phonetic components.

components.text: The whole graph pictures light and flames rising from a burning object and represents fire. It has no smaller components or internal sound cue.

history.text: The curated Shang oracle-bone examples show different forms of 火, illustrating variation without establishing a sequence between them. The graph is analyzed as depicting light and flames from a burning object. Warring States forms are described as linearized into four strokes while retaining a suggestion of rising flame. The cited collection contains no bronze form, which does not prove that no bronze example exists elsewhere.
A Han-period lexicographic account also describes flames rising and classifies 火 as a pictogram; this is a later explanation, not direct evidence for the Shang graph’s origin.

uncertainties.text: The cited oracle-bone examples establish Shang-period use, but their individual dates are unresolved. The selected images are modern vector renderings of catalogued forms, not artifact photographs.
Competing Old Chinese reconstructions and proposed inherited comparisons remain unresolved; the proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison is specifically described as phonologically problematic.

senses.gloss: a star name, 大火 (Antares / 心宿二)
senses.period: Shang-period oracle-bone use; also attested in the Classic of Poetry
senses.text: 火 is attested as a star name in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and later in the Classic of Poetry. The 字源 passage tentatively calls it 火星; the CUHK entries identify the referent as 大火/心宿二. The sources do not explain why the star was called 火.
The modern Mandarin dictionary records 火 as a verb meaning ‘burn’; its date and historical relation to the noun ‘fire’ are unresolved.
The modern Mandarin dictionary records 火 in a verb use meaning ‘become angry’; its date and historical relation to the noun ‘fire’ are unresolved.

limitations.text: The star-name use is distinct from the literal sense ‘fire’. 字源 tentatively calls the star 火星, while the CUHK entries identify the referent as 大火/心宿二. The evidence does not explain why the star was called 火 or how its name relates to ‘fire’.
The supplied glosses do not establish when ‘burn’ or ‘anger/rage’ arose or how they relate to ‘fire’.

One interpretation reads 火 in an oracle-bone context as a phonetic loan for 禍 ‘calamity’: the sign would have been reused for a different word because the words were thought to sound similar. The proposal is based on sound proximity and context, but no independently checked sound comparison is supplied.

limitations.text: These are modern vector renderings of glyphs catalogued from oracle-bone records, not photographs of artifacts. The cited examples are Shang-period, but their individual archaeological dates are not established here.
The rising-flame reading is a scholarly analysis of the graph; the shapes alone do not establish its historical meaning.
